clinicalPearls: Classically follows severe trauma, particularly head injury, chest compression or long-bone fracture, with sudden visual loss developing shortly afterwards
The non-traumatic Purtscher-like form accompanies acute pancreatitis, renal failure, connective tissue disease, amniotic fluid embolism and childbirth
The fundus shows multiple cotton-wool spots and areas of superficial retinal whitening clustered around the optic disc, frequently bilateral
Purtscher flecken, polygonal patches of inner retinal whitening lying between arterioles and venules with a clear zone flanking the vessels, are highly characteristic
Retinal haemorrhages are usually few relative to the extent of ischaemic whitening
Fluorescein angiography demonstrates arteriolar and capillary non-perfusion in the affected areas
There is no proven ocular treatment, so care is directed at the underlying systemic cause and supportive observation
reference.pathophysiology: The retinopathy results from occlusion of retinal arterioles and precapillary vessels by microemboli, which may consist of fat, air, fibrin or aggregated leucocytes. Complement activation with generation of C5a is thought to cause leucocyte aggregation and leucoembolisation, a mechanism particularly implicated in acute pancreatitis. The resulting precapillary arteriolar occlusion produces the ischaemic cotton-wool spots and polygonal Purtscher flecken seen around the posterior pole.
additionalDifferentials: Non-accidental injury with retinal haemorrhages in a child
additionalInvestigations: Dilated fundus examination to identify cotton-wool spots and Purtscher flecken
Fluorescein angiography to map arteriolar occlusion and capillary non-perfusion
Optical coherence tomography to document inner retinal ischaemic changes
Serum amylase and lipase when pancreatitis is suspected
Renal function tests and an autoimmune screen for a systemic precipitant
Detailed history for recent trauma or an obstetric or systemic trigger
redFlags: An underlying life-threatening cause such as acute pancreatitis or systemic embolism
Associated systemic decompensation requiring urgent medical care
Suspicion of non-accidental injury in a child
reference.prognosis: The visual outcome is variable; some eyes recover partially over weeks to months as the ischaemic whitening resolves, while others are left with permanent central or field loss and subsequent optic atrophy.
pitfalls: Missing the underlying systemic precipitant in the non-traumatic form
Attributing the picture to direct ocular trauma alone
Confusing the retinal whitening with commotio retinae
Failing to recognise Purtscher flecken as a distinctive sign
references: American Academy of Ophthalmology, Basic and Clinical Science Course: Retina and Vitreous
